title: Design Text Editor
description:
# Design Text Editor

Design a text editor with a cursor.

The cursor sits between characters. Text can be inserted at the cursor, characters immediately to the left of the cursor can be deleted, and the cursor can move left or right without crossing the beginning or the end of the document.

Implement the `TextEditor` class:

*   `TextEditor()` initializes an empty editor with the cursor at the beginning.
*   `void addText(String text)` inserts `text` at the cursor. After insertion, the cursor is immediately to the right of the inserted text.
*   `int deleteText(int k)` deletes up to `k` characters immediately to the left of the cursor, like pressing backspace repeatedly. It returns the number of characters actually deleted.
*   `String cursorLeft(int k)` moves the cursor left up to `k` positions and returns the last `min(10, len)` characters to the left of the cursor, where `len` is the number of characters to the left of the cursor after the move.
*   `String cursorRight(int k)` moves the cursor right up to `k` positions and returns the last `min(10, len)` characters to the left of the cursor after the move.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input**
["TextEditor", "addText", "deleteText", "addText", "cursorRight", "cursorLeft", "deleteText", "cursorLeft", "cursorRight"]
[[], ["leetcode"], [4], ["practice"], [3], [8], [10], [2], [6]]
**Output**
[null, null, 4, null, "etpractice", "leet", 4, "", "practi"]
**Explanation**
After adding `leetcode`, deleting 4 characters leaves `leet`. Adding `practice` at the cursor gives `leetpractice`. Moving right at the end keeps the cursor at the end and returns the last 10 characters. Moving left, deleting, and moving again must preserve the cursor position and surrounding text exactly.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= text.length, k <= 40`
*   `text` consists of lowercase English letters.
*   At most `2 * 10^4` calls will be made to `addText`, `deleteText`, `cursorLeft`, and `cursorRight`.

## Follow-up:

Can you make every operation run in `O(k)` time, where `k` is the input argument length or movement distance?

solutions.name: Two StringBuilder Halves
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep the text left of the cursor in one `StringBuilder` in normal order. Keep the text right of the cursor in another `StringBuilder` in reverse order, so the nearest character to the right of the cursor is at the end. Moving the cursor transfers characters between the two builders.

## Key Insight

Only the area near the cursor changes. Storing both sides separately makes insertion and backspace operations happen at the end of a builder, and cursor movement only moves the requested number of boundary characters.

## Complexity Analysis

Adding or moving `k` characters costs O(k), deletion costs O(k), and returning the last 10 left-side characters is O(1). Space is O(n).

solutions.name: Single StringBuilder with Cursor Index
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n + k) per insertion/deletion in the worst case
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store the whole document in one `StringBuilder` and keep an integer cursor position. Inserting and deleting use the builder's indexed operations. Cursor movement clamps the cursor inside `[0, length]`, and the return value is a substring ending at the cursor.

## Key Insight

This baseline mirrors the problem statement directly. Although middle insertions and deletions may shift many characters, the explicit cursor index is easy to reason about and is useful for validating more advanced designs.

## Complexity Analysis

Moving the cursor and producing the 10-character view is O(1), but insertion or deletion in the middle can be O(n + k) because characters shift. Space is O(n).

solutions.name: Doubly Linked List Cursor
solutions.description:
## Approach

Represent every character as a node in a doubly linked list with head and tail sentinels. Keep `cursor` as the node immediately to the left of the cursor position. Insertions add nodes after `cursor`, backspace removes nodes ending at `cursor`, and movement walks the linked list.

## Key Insight

The cursor is not a character; it is a boundary between characters. Keeping the node immediately to the left of that boundary makes insertion, deletion, and movement local operations.

## Complexity Analysis

Each inserted, deleted, or moved character is touched once, so every operation costs O(k). Returning the 10-character view walks at most 10 nodes. Space is O(n).

solutions.name: Gap Buffer
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a character array with an empty gap at the cursor. Characters before the gap are left of the cursor; characters after the gap are right of the cursor. Moving the cursor shifts characters across the gap. Inserting fills the gap, and deletion widens the gap to the left.

## Key Insight

A gap buffer is a classic text-editor structure. It keeps edits near the cursor cheap because insertion and deletion happen by changing the gap rather than shifting the whole document each time.

## Complexity Analysis

Moving or deleting `k` characters is O(k). Insertion is O(k) amortized because the underlying buffer grows only when the gap is too small. Space is O(n).

solutions.name: Implicit Treap Rope
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store the document as an implicit treap: an ordered tree whose in-order traversal is the text, and whose node sizes allow splitting by cursor position. Insertions split at the cursor and merge in the inserted text. Deletion splits out the removed range. Cursor movement changes only the cursor index.

## Key Insight

The treap route treats the document as a sequence with efficient split and merge operations. It is heavier than a gap buffer, but it teaches how editor buffers can scale beyond local cursor edits.

## Complexity Analysis

Splits and merges cost O(log n) expected time. Collecting the view touches at most 10 characters, and building inserted text touches its length. Space is O(n).
